profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting at an academic health system evaluating a draft proposal for implementing the SF-36 in a digital orthopedic recovery program. The proposal covers how patients will complete the survey through the patient portal, how non-responders will be contacted by phone, and how scores will flow into a clinician dashboard and research export. The agenda is to review whether the current design is acceptable for the upcoming pilot, focusing on timing of administration, scoring behavior, and support for alternate administration modes. The expected outcome is an apparent go-ahead on the design with a few follow-up actions, even though the two reviewers quietly leave with different assumptions about what exactly was approved.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.expertise: Psychometrics, clinical outcomes measurement, longitudinal survey design
members.background: Lena leads outcomes instrument selection for musculoskeletal studies and has previously used SF-36 in multi-site rehabilitation research with paper, phone, and clinic administration.
members.private_state: She wants the implementation approved only if it preserves measurement comparability across sites and modes, because she plans to use the pilot data for a later outcomes publication and does not want to reopen scoring or mode-equivalence issues after launch.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'baseline,' they mean the SF-36 completed before any meaningful clinical intervention, not merely the first survey obtained after enrollment.

If a team says it will use 'standard scoring,' that means the manual-based SF-36 subscale scoring rules she normally uses, with transparent missing-item handling and no extra vendor-generated summary outputs unless explicitly specified.
A 'telephone administration' of SF-36 is only valid if a trained interviewer reads the items verbatim and the mode is tracked separately from self-administration.
References to 'the pilot' mean the planned three-site rehab outcomes pilot, because that is the program context in which she has been discussing the instrument.

members.name: Evan Brooks
members.expertise: Patient portal workflows, clinical operations rollout, vendor integrations
members.background: Evan manages questionnaire deployment inside the health system's patient app and is responsible for getting surveys into live workflows with minimal staff burden and stable dashboard reporting.
members.private_state: He wants a practical approval that lets his team keep the launch date, relying on existing portal modules and care-coordinator workflows rather than introducing special-case scripts, mode flags, or custom scoring logic that would slow implementation.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'baseline,' they mean the patient's first captured SF-36 in the system during the enrollment window, even if it happens after the initial clinic visit.
If the proposal says 'standard scoring,' it refers to the vendor's built-in SF-36 scoring package, including its default handling of partial responses and automatic summary outputs.
A 'telephone option' simply means staff can call a patient, read the questions naturally, and enter responses into the same portal workflow used for self-completion.
Mentions of 'the pilot' refer to the first live deployment at the downtown orthopedic clinic, with other sites added later once the workflow proves stable.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to collecting a 'baseline SF-36' before tracking follow-up changes.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a pre-treatment measure collected before surgery, therapy, or other substantive intervention begins.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the first SF-36 successfully captured in the system during onboarding, even if the patient completes it later the same day or after the first visit.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are discussing longitudinal comparison, and in many programs the first captured survey often happens close enough to treatment start that the phrase 'baseline' feels self-evident and does not invite clarification.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the implementation will use 'standard SF-36 scoring.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes manual-style SF-36 scoring: item recoding, 0-100 scale transformation, scale calculation only under the usual item-completeness rules, and no automatic PCS/MCS summaries unless separately agreed.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the vendor's SF-36 module counts as standard: it computes available subscales and summary outputs using its built-in missing-data rules and preconfigured dashboard fields.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Each sees their own scoring pathway as the obvious default behind the phrase 'standard,' and a design review focused on workflow usually would not drill into library settings unless a visible discrepancy had already occurred.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the design should support a 'telephone option' for patients who do not complete the portal form.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this includes a trained interviewer protocol, verbatim item wording, neutral prompting rules, and mode labeling so phone-administered data can be interpreted correctly.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes it simply means care coordinators can call patients and enter answers into the same questionnaire flow without extra scripting, training, or separate mode metadata.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: At the surface level both are solving the same operational problem of nonresponse, and the phrase 'telephone option' sounds like a straightforward access feature rather than a design choice with methodological boundaries.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether the design is 'ready for the pilot.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the named three-site rehab outcomes pilot that will use SF-36 data comparatively across locations.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the one-site downtown clinic soft launch that product and operations have been calling the pilot in internal rollout decks.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both projects are temporally adjacent and repeatedly labeled just 'the pilot' in meetings and slide headers, so the shared phrase creates a false sense of referential alignment.

turns.inner_thought: Before I sign off, I need confidence that the three-site rehab outcomes pilot will generate publishable SF-36 data without forcing us to revisit mode equivalence or scoring later. Baseline has to mean before any meaningful intervention begins, standard scoring needs to be the manual-based scale scoring I normally use, and the telephone option has to be methodologically defensible if those data are going into the pilot export.
turns.utterance: I wanted to use this review to confirm the SF-36 design is ready for the pilot, especially around baseline capture, standard scoring, and the telephone option if patients don't complete the portal form.

turns.inner_thought: This should be a straightforward approval for the downtown clinic launch. We already have the portal module configured to send the SF-36 at onboarding, then repeat it on the follow-up schedule. The vendor's built-in package is what I consider standard scoring, and the easiest path for the telephone option is letting coordinators call and enter answers in the same workflow so we don't create special cases.
turns.utterance: From the product side, the proposal is pretty simple: we send the SF-36 at onboarding, keep the later follow-ups on the standard cadence, use standard scoring, and give coordinators a telephone option for anyone who doesn't finish in the app.

turns.inner_thought: The cadence itself sounds fine if the first measure is truly pre-treatment. My main concern is that once people start talking about change over time, everyone assumes baseline was handled correctly, and then it's too late to fix. If that piece is secure, the rest is manageable.
turns.utterance: The cadence looks reasonable to me as long as the baseline SF-36 is in place before we start making follow-up comparisons.

turns.inner_thought: Right, baseline is just the first captured survey during enrollment. Since enrollment begins after the first visit in our workflow, patients might complete it later that day, or a coordinator may get it by phone if they miss the portal prompt. That's still baseline in the system and keeps operations moving.
turns.utterance: That should work with the current flow. Enrollment starts after the first visit, and patients can still complete the baseline form later that day or through a coordinator call if needed.

turns.inner_thought: I need reassurance that phone-collected responses won't quietly get mixed in without any attention to consistency. If the telephone option is handled properly and then standard scoring is applied in the usual way, I can live with some flexibility on outreach. I don't want to ask a long methodological question in this meeting, but I do want to hear that the process is controlled.
turns.utterance: Okay. On the phone fallback, is the telephone option set up so those responses can still be treated consistently once standard scoring is applied?

turns.inner_thought: Yes, in the operational sense. Coordinators can just call, read the questions as needed, and key responses into the same portal questionnaire. No separate scripts, no extra fields, no branching logic. Using the same workflow is exactly how we preserve what I think of as standard scoring and avoid delaying launch.
turns.utterance: Yes, that's the idea. Coordinators would read the questions as needed and enter the answers into the same workflow, which keeps it simple and should preserve standard scoring.

turns.inner_thought: For the three-site pilot export, I need the eight SF-36 subscales available cleanly so I can evaluate patterns across sites and modes and score them the way I expect. If scoring is finalized appropriately, the export should support analysis without forcing me into opaque summaries.
turns.utterance: Good. For the pilot export, I would expect the eight SF-36 scales to come through cleanly once scoring is finalized.

turns.inner_thought: The main thing our stakeholders want in the dashboard is the usual physical and mental summaries, and the vendor package already generates those. It also handles incomplete submissions automatically, which is helpful because we don't want records dropped just because a patient skipped an item or two. If Lena wants the scale-level fields in the export, I assume those can sit alongside the standard outputs.
turns.utterance: That aligns with what the module produces. The dashboard will show the usual physical and mental summaries, and it can score most partial submissions automatically as well.

turns.inner_thought: I still want to verify details in the build, but at a high level this sounds acceptable for the three pilot sites if baseline, phone coverage, and scoring are all accounted for. I'll treat today as conceptual approval and make sure the export is reviewed before data collection starts.
turns.utterance: All right. With baseline, the telephone option, and scoring apparently accounted for, this sounds ready for the pilot sites from my perspective.

turns.inner_thought: Great, that's enough to keep the downtown soft launch on track. I'll tell the team we have approval to proceed with launch prep using the existing portal workflow, coordinator call process, and vendor scoring package. We can train staff next and avoid reopening design questions.
turns.utterance: Great, then I'll move ahead with launch prep and coordinator training for the pilot based on today's review, and we'll keep the remaining follow-ups to the implementation details.
